messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm doing a path analysis with a set of observed variables. As a first step I made a saturated model and the I dropped my non-significant paths (p>0.1).

My initial model was this:
ww1 <- 'ww ~ smi + ug + fdb + sex + seas
                  smi ~ sex + seas
                  ug ~ smi + sex + seas
                  fdb ~ smi + ug + sex + seas
                  seas ~~ 0*sex'

And my final path model looks like this:
ww3 <- 'ww ~ ug + seas
          ug ~ sex + seas
          fdb ~ ug + seas
          seas ~~ 0*sex
          ww ~~ 0*fdb'

"sex" and "seas" are two level exogenous dummy variables. I do not want the to be correlated.
But note the last line from my final model (ww3). If I don't add that line (ww ~~ 0*fdb), lavaan automatically correlates "ww" with "fdb", although I don't want that.
Why is he doing that? Is this the right way to handle this issue?

Thank you in advance!

Attila

I'm exploring Rasch and binary CFA to understand how they align. For Rasch modeling, I use Winsteps. I planned on doing two things:

easier to use labels; equal labels imply equal parameter values, eg:

x <- '

           a*LDPAR702 +
           a*LDPAR613 +

           a*LDPAR773 +
           a*LDPAR694 +
           a*LDPAR697 +
           a*LDPAR716 +
           a*LDPAR691 +
           a*LDPAR771
'

(and not the single quotes instead of the double quotes, although the
latter will work too in most circumstances).

messages.subject_clean: user-supplied baseline model
messages.body_plain:
Hello Yves,

I'd like to suggest the addition of a new argument to the lavaan function that would allow the user to override the default baseline model (perhaps similar to the slotParTable argument).  In multiple-group and longitudinal models, a more restrictive baseline model may be more appropriate for calculating incremental fit indices than the traditional independence model, which allows variances/means of variables to differ across groups/occasions.  Or in the case of latent growth curve models, a common constraint (although often an unnecessary one) is to constrain the residual variances to equality over time.  In such a case, the traditional independence model is not nested within the (albeit less restrictive) hypothesized model, so it is not an appropriate baseline model for calculating CFI.  Bentler & Satorra's (2010) Nesting/Equivalence Testing method can verify this, using the code below.

Thank you for all your work on lavaan!

Terry

growthModel <- '
# intercept and slope with fixed coefficients
i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4
s =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 3*t4
t1 ~~ e*t1
t2 ~~ e*t2
t3 ~~ e*t3
t4 ~~ e*t4
'

growthFit <- growth(growthModel, data = Demo.growth)
summary(growthFit, fit = TRUE)

baselineModel <- '
t1 ~~ t1
t2 ~~ t2
t3 ~~ t3
t4 ~~ t4
t1 + t2 + t3 + t4 ~ 1
'
baseFit <- growth(baselineModel, data = Demo.growth)
summary(baseFit, fit = TRUE)

base.sigma <- baseFit@Fi...@Sigma.hat[[1]]
base.mu <http://base.mu> <- as.numeric(baseFit@Fi...@Mu.hat[[1]])
rownames(base.sigma) <- paste0("t", 1:4)
colnames(base.sigma) <- paste0("t", 1:4)
names(base.mu <http://base.mu>) <- paste0("t", 1:4)
base.sigma
base.mu <http://base.mu>

## if the baseModel were nested within the growthModel, its model-implied
## moments could be perfectly reproduced by the growthModel (i.e., chi-sq = 0)
nestedTest <- growth(growthModel, sample.cov = base.sigma, sample.mean = base.mu <http://base.mu>,
                     std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, sample.nobs = nrow(Demo.growth))
summary(nestedTest, fit = TRUE)

If estimator="MLR", you get two RMSEAs: the usual one (based on standard
X2) and one based on the scaled X2. The latter one uses an adjusted
value for the degrees of freedom:

# usual
RMSEA <- sqrt( max( c((X2/N)/df - 1/(N-GG), 0) ) ) * sqrt(G)

# scaled
RMSEA.scaled <- sqrt( max( c((X2/N)/d - 1/(N-GG), 0) ) ) * sqrt(G)
# where d <- sum(object@Fit@test[[2]]$trace.UGamma)

But both currently (0.5-14) use 'N' (as in the total number of rows in
the data). Perhaps this needs revision. Do you know of a paper
discussing this?

messages.body_plain:
Okay, I've pinpointed the problem playing with some of my own data. The issue is in the specification of the higher order factors. Currently, when higher order factors are specified using the =~ operator to define the higher order factor kicks back an error (this stems from the specification of the null and saturated models used when computing model fit indices). I'll put this on the list of issues to fix.

Fortunately there's an easy fix. Just switch the =~ operator to ~ for the second order factors and (with a few other adjustments) you should be all set.

So this:

2ndOrderF1 =~ 1stOrderF1.a + 1stOrderF1.b
2ndOrderF2 =~ 1stOrderF2.a + 1stOrderF2.b
2ndOrderF3 =~ 1stOrderF3.a + 1stOrderF3.b

Becomes:
#Specify 2nd order latents with a loading of 0
#Trick to estimate the model
2ndOrderF1 =~ 0*ind10
2ndOrderF2 =~ 0*ind10
2ndOrderF3 =~ 0*ind10

#Use regression instead of loading operator
1stOrderF1.a ~  1*2ndOrderF1
1stOrderF1.b ~  2ndOrderF1
1stOrderF2.a ~ 1*2ndOrderF2
1stOrderF2.b ~ 2ndOrderF2
1stOrderF3.a ~ 1*2ndOrderF3
1stOrderF3.b ~ 2ndOrderF3

#don't allow 1st order factors to covary (as is default)
1stOrderF1.a ~~ 0*1stOrderF1.b + 0*1stOrderF2.a + 0*1stOrderF2.b + 0*1stOrderF3.a + 0*1stOrderF3.b
1stOrderF1.b ~~ 0*1stOrderF2.a + 0*1stOrderF2.b + 0*1stOrderF3.a + 0*1stOrderF3.b
1stOrderF2.a ~~ 0*1stOrderF2.b + 0*1stOrderF3.a + 0*1stOrderF3.b
1stOrderF2.b ~~ 0*1stOrderF3.a + 0*1stOrderF3.b
1stOrderF3.a ~~ 0*1stOrderF3.b

>

> something like:
>
> x1 ~*~ c(d1,d1,d1)*x1
> x2 ~*~ c(d2,d2,d2)*x2
> x2 ~*~ c(d3,d3,d3)*x2
> ...
>
> In this example, I have assumed three groups. By setting the labels
> equal across groups, the delta factors will be constrained to be equal.
>
> Yves.

messages.body_plain:
On the midterm exam in my class, I gave students a model and a dataset with missing data.  Besides its other features, the model specified an equality constraint for two parameters--reciprocal relations linking factors F4 and F5.  My version of the syntax for this was:
'
          F1 =~ Y1+Y2+Y3
          F2 =~ Y4
          F3 =~ Y5+Y6
          F4 =~ Y7+Y8+Y9
          F5 =~ Y10+Y11

          F5 ~ mike*F4+F1
          F4 ~ mike*F5+F2+F3

          F4 ~~F5
          F1 ~~0*F3
          F2 ~~0*F3
          Y4~~0.20*Y4
'
     With the sem function and missing = "FIML" I got the expected result--the simulated data fits this model well.
     One of my students specified the equality constraint differently:
'
          F5 ~ b1*F4+F1
          F4 ~ b2*F5+F2+F3

          b1 == b2
'
     This specification produced error messages.  The parameters constrained to equality went to an extreme value (-1.001) such that Sigma-hat was not positive definite.

     Should the student's syntax have worked?  I am attaching the data file, which has 999 for a missing value code.  The file also has an extra 12th column of 1s.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I would appreciate conceptual and technical help thinking through an analysis.

Conceptual

Let's say I have the following 5 models I want to test for a fake 9-item ordinal dataset (run the code below to plot with semPlot for visual diagrams):

A. 1 first-order factor (f0)
B. 3 first order correlated factors (f1, f2, f3)
C. 3 first order correlated factors (f1, f2, f3) with two cross-loading items on f1 and f2
D. hierarchical: 1 second-order factor (g), 3 first-order uncorrelated factors (f1, f2, f3)
E. bifactor: 1 general factor (g) and 3 first-order uncorrelated factors (f1, f2, f3)

I believe the nesting is as follows:
A within B (constrain factor correlations to get A)
B within C (constrain cross-loadings of C to get B)
D within B (second-order nested within first-order correlated factors models)
D within E (per Yung et al., 1999 <http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02294531>)

Question 1: Is the above nesting correct?
Question 2: Is D also nested with C? If D is within B, and B is within C, then I think D should also be within C.

Technical

Let's assume I am correct about the nesting and shift to programming. I created a reproducible example here <http://rpubs.com/ericpgreen/9923> that shows all five models.

Question 3: Do the models look like they are specified correctly in lavaan? Any suggested improvements to the specifications to match the descriptions of each model?

Thanks for considering this request.

Eric

<Chime in>
This is 100% correct (for the current version of lavaan, 0.5-14): as
soon as "==" or "<" or ">" statements are added to the model syntax,
lavaan 'switches' to the constrained optimizer (nlminb.constr), which is
very, very sensitive to starting values.

This was in fact designed to handle ugly highly-nonlinear (in)equality
constraints, like b1 == exp(b2)^2 + log(b3 + b4).

What lavaan is not doing (yet), is to 'catch' simple linear equality
constraints (like b1 == 2*b2), because in this case, we can simply
reduce the problem using a projection matrix, and everything will run
smoothly. This is happening already when we have 'equal labels', but we
need to extend this to all linear equality constraints (specified by
using the '==' operator). More work to do.
</Chime in>

Yves.

Internally, lavaan stores all numbers in double precision. Only when
printing to the screen, only 3 digits after the decimal point are shown.
For the 'summary()' function, there is currently no way to change this.
However, for the parameterEstimates() function, you can use this:

as.data.frame( unclass( parameterEstimates(fit) ) )

or extract the parameters as a column ('est'):

parameterEstimates(fit)$est

Or, you can use coef(), together with unclass:

unclass( coef(fit) )

This gives you the parameter labels too. (The 'unclass()' function
removes the 'lavaan.*' class that determines the printing style)

messages.body_plain:
> I originally was using MANOVA to test the difference between groups, but our local stats guru suggested using path modeling via lavaan instead.
>

Well, the answer depends on what hypotheses you want to test.  If you were original looking at MANOVA, then you might only be interested in comparing the mean vectors across groups.  If that is the case, then this is certainly a decent alternative to MANOVA because you don't have to make the restrictive assumption of sphericity.  Also, MANOVA has differential power to detect group differences in a mean vector depending on the degree and direction of correlation among DVs (e.g., low power when positively correlated, high power when negatively correlated, obviously more complex when you have more than 2 DVs).

> There aren't any latent variables specified, just one manifest exogenous variable and then the 11 endogenous ones.  The model I have runs just fine, but it's with Group set as an ordinal variables with C G S converted to 0 1 2.  That output shows me that there's a significant change in my endogenous variables as Group 'increases' (ie. goes from C to G to S), but I don't know how to evaluate the magnitude of the effect of shifting from one Group category to the next.  (Ie. is the significance being driven by the increase from C to G, or from G to S?  And what is happening at each level?)
>

I would caution against treating your grouping variable as though it were continuous.  You are currently estimating a regression slope for each DV that describes the change in that DV with each unit-increase in the group variable (i.e., identical change between C and G as there is between G and S).  That is a restrictive assumption, and there is no reason to make it.  Graphs of the means show that assumption might be a reasonable for a couple DVs (e.g., wf, we, mf), but you should consider whether you want to make that assumption.

a.data <- read.csv("a_data.csv")
head(a.data)
## save names of dependent variables
DVs <- c("vis.pain","mi","dexterity","wf","we","mf","me","pain","ltd.fxn","swelling","stiffness")

## view mean differences across group to check whether trends are linear
par(mfrow = c(4, 3))
for (i in DVs) {
  myFormula <- as.formula(paste(i, "group", sep = " ~ "))
  groupMeans <- aggregate(myFormula, data = a.data, mean)
  plot(groupMeans)
  lines(groupMeans)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

> I'm not sure if the multiple groups option can help me get traction on this - someone suggested using this argument, but it seems like that's more appropriate to employ when you have the same model that you'd like to test in different samples.  In this case, I'd be changing the actual model - breaking down the exogenous variable into three groups, and then all I'd have to compare would be the covariances between my endogenous variables...which doesn't seem quite right.
>

That's true, but only because you have not included the mean structure in your model.  You can add the mean structure, and test whether the mean vector differs across groups in a multiple-group model.  You can just take the regression out of your current syntax, in which case you are specifying a saturated covariance matrix in each group -- you can also specify a saturated covariance structure pretty quickly/automatically using the code below:

myModel <- outer(DVs, DVs, function(x, y) paste(x, "~~", y))[lower.tri(diag(DVs), diag = TRUE)]
myModel <- paste(myModel, collapse = "\n")
cat(myModel)
## you can specify the saturated mean structure in a lavaan argument (int.ov.free = TRUE)
## or you can specify the saturated mean structure in the syntax:
# myModel <- outer(DVs, DVs, function(x, y) paste(x, "~~", y))[lower.tri(diag(DVs), diag = TRUE)]
# myModel <- paste(c(myModel, paste(DVs, "~", 1, collapse = "\n")), collapse = "\n")
# cat(myModel)

You can then fit that model to your data, but specifying the grouping variable in the "group" argument of your call to the lavaan function:

allFree <- lavaan(myModel, data = a.data, int.ov.free = TRUE, group = "group")

This allows all means to be equal across group, and because it is saturated, the chi-squared fit statistic is 0 (no constraints means no hypotheses to test).  Any null hypotheses you want to test simply requires you to make those constraints.  For instance, the omnibus MANOVA test that the mean vector is equal in all groups can be specified using the "group.equal" argument:

omniFit <- lavaan(myModel, data = a.data, int.ov.free = TRUE, group = "group", group.equal = "intercepts")
## chi-square test of significance rejects that null hypothesis, so group differences exist
inspect(omniFit, "fit")[c("chisq", "df", "pvalue")]

Any follow-up tests require specifying the mean structure directly in your syntax using labels to constrain a specific parameter across specific groups.  I attached a lavaan script showing an example of follow-up tests (analogous to MANOVA, as I would conduct them) for one DV.  I hope it helps.  Let me know if you have questions about it.

Terry

> B. 3 first order correlated factors (f1, f2, f3)

> I believe the nesting is as follows:
> A within B (constrain factor correlations to get A)
> B within C (constrain cross-loadings of C to get B)
> D within B (second-order nested within first-order correlated factors models)
> D within E (per Yung et al., 1999 <http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02294531>)
>
> Question 1: Is the above nesting correct?
> Question 2: Is D also nested with C? If D is within B, and B is within C, then I think D should also be within C.
>
>

Eric,

For some time, I have been meaning to write a function for the semTools package to implement tests for nesting and equivalence, using Bentler & Satorra's (2010) method (see attached PDF).  This motivates me to get it done soon.  Below is the "engine" for that function, which will test whether model "x" is nested within model "y" -- bearing in mind that model equivalence is a special case of nesting when the nested models have equal degrees of freedom (or equivalently, the same number of parameter estimates).  You can use this function to test your models, one pair at a time, for nesting/equivalence by passing your fitted lavaan objects to the model (e.g., fit.mod.A and fit.mod.B):

x.within.y <- function(x, y, crit = .0001) {
  require(lavaan)
  prepCov <- function(x, varNames) {
    for (g in seq_along(x)) {
      colnames(x[[g]]) <- varNames[[g]]
      rownames(x[[g]]) <- varNames[[g]]
    }
    x
  }
  prepMu <- function(x, varNames) {
    for (g in seq_along(x)) {
      x[[g]] <- as.numeric(x[[g]])
      names(x[[g]]) <- varNames[[g]]
    }
    x
  }

  ## check the data information matches (e.g., sample sizes)
  if (!identical(x@Data, y@Data)) stop("Models must apply to the same data")

  ## variable names
  if (identical(x@pta$vnames$ov, y@pta$vnames$ov)) {
    varNames <- x@pta$vnames$ov
  } else {
    stop("Models do not contain the same variables")
  }

  ## check degrees of freedom support nesting structure
  if (inspect(x, "fit")["df"] < inspect(y, "fit")["df"]) stop("
      x cannot be nested within y because y is more restricted than x")

  ## model-implied moments
  Sigma <- prepCov(x@Fi...@Sigma.hat, varNames)
  Mu <- prepMu(x@Fi...@Mu.hat, varNames)

  ## fit model and inspect chi-squared
  myFit <- lavaan(sample.cov = Sigma, sample.mean = Mu, sample.nobs = x@Data@nobs,
                  slotParTable = y@ParTable, slotModel = y@Model, slotOptions = y@Options)
  result <- inspect(myFit, "fit")["chisq"] < crit
  names(result) <- NULL
  if (inspect(x, "fit")["df"] == inspect(y, "fit")["df"]) return(c(Equivalent = result))
  c(Nested = result)
}

Also attached is an R script that includes this function and some examples to run, so you can see how it works.

Soon, I'll submit a more generic function to semTools that will accept any number of fitted lavaan objects, sort them according to the number of degrees of freedom, make the necessary tests, and return a logical matrix indicating the nesting/equivalence relationships.  I might make it general enough that you could simply pass model syntax as well, in which case the function would simulate data for the tests, as described in Bentler & Satorra (2010).  Watch this space :-)

Terry

What out of bounds estimate are you talking about?  If this is the model-implied covariance matrix, you can't tell whether there are out of bounds estimates very easily -- try cov2cor() to turn it into a correlation matrix, and see if there are any values that exceed [1, -1].

If this is the sample covariance matrix, you can do the same cov2cor() check, but you might have out of bounds estimates because you have missing data, IF this sample matrix is estimated using pairwise deletion (instead of extracting the ML estimate from lavaan).

If the correlations among your variables are as low as they seem from the covariance matrix, I wouldn't trust results from any package, unless you have a very large sample size and use more items to identify your constructs, in order to compensate for the low communalities (see attached article for advice).  But it's hard to tell whether this is a problem from your (unstandardized) covariance matrix.  It's also worth noting that you have some wildly different variances among the indicators within each construct (e.g., 2.8 vs. 0.03, or 7.25 vs. 0.48).  That can cause problems, so you might consider rescaling your variables in some way to make their variances more similar.  I don't have a specific guideline, but certainly the variables with more than 10 times, and some close to 100 times, greater variance than other indicators would be problematic (although I'm not sure it's related to why you get different numbers in the two packages).

It's also possible you still aren't specifying the exact same model in both packages.  Have you checked your degrees of freedom and number of parameters being estimated?

On Sunday, October 27, 2013 at 2:20 PM, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:

>
>
> >
> > A. 1 first-order factor (f0)
> > B. 3 first order correlated factors (f1, f2, f3)
> > C. 3 first order correlated factors (f1, f2, f3) with two cross-loading items on f1 and f2
> > D. hierarchical: 1 second-order factor (g), 3 first-order uncorrelated factors (f1, f2, f3)
> > E. bifactor: 1 general factor (g) and 3 first-order uncorrelated factors (f1, f2, f3)
> >
> > I believe the nesting is as follows:
> > A within B (constrain factor correlations to get A)
> > B within C (constrain cross-loadings of C to get B)
> > D within B (second-order nested within first-order correlated factors models)
> > D within E (per Yung et al., 1999 <http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02294531>)
> >
> > Question 1: Is the above nesting correct?
> > Question 2: Is D also nested with C? If D is within B, and B is within C, then I think D should also be within C.
> >
> >

>
> Eric,
>
> For some time, I have been meaning to write a function for the semTools package to implement tests for nesting and equivalence, using Bentler & Satorra's (2010) method (see attached PDF).  This motivates me to get it done soon.  Below is the "engine" for that function, which will test whether model "x" is nested within model "y" -- bearing in mind that model equivalence is a special case of nesting when the nested models have equal degrees of freedom (or equivalently, the same number of parameter estimates).  You can use this function to test your models, one pair at a time, for nesting/equivalence by passing your fitted lavaan objects to the model (e.g., fit.mod.A and fit.mod.B):
>

> x.within.y <- function(x, y, crit = .0001) {
>   require(lavaan)
>   prepCov <- function(x, varNames) {
>     for (g in seq_along(x)) {
>       colnames(x[[g]]) <- varNames[[g]]
>       rownames(x[[g]]) <- varNames[[g]]
>     }
>     x
>   }
>   prepMu <- function(x, varNames) {
>     for (g in seq_along(x)) {
>       x[[g]] <- as.numeric(x[[g]])
>       names(x[[g]]) <- varNames[[g]]
>     }
>     x
>   }
>
>   ## check the data information matches (e.g., sample sizes)
>   if (!identical(x@Data, y@Data)) stop("Models must apply to the same data")
>
>   ## variable names
>   if (identical(x@pta$vnames$ov, y@pta$vnames$ov)) {
>     varNames <- x@pta$vnames$ov
>   } else {
>     stop("Models do not contain the same variables")
>   }
>
>   ## check degrees of freedom support nesting structure
>   if (inspect(x, "fit")["df"] < inspect(y, "fit")["df"]) stop("
>       x cannot be nested within y because y is more restricted than x")
>
>   ## model-implied moments

>   Sigma <- prepCov(x@F...@Sigma.hat, varNames)
>   Mu <- prepMu(x@F...@Mu.hat, varNames)

>
>
>   ## fit model and inspect chi-squared
>   myFit <- lavaan(sample.cov = Sigma, sample.mean = Mu, sample.nobs = x@Data@nobs,
>                   slotParTable = y@ParTable, slotModel = y@Model, slotOptions = y@Options)
>   result <- inspect(myFit, "fit")["chisq"] < crit
>   names(result) <- NULL
>   if (inspect(x, "fit")["df"] == inspect(y, "fit")["df"]) return(c(Equivalent = result))
>   c(Nested = result)
> }

>
> Also attached is an R script that includes this function and some examples to run, so you can see how it works.
>
> Soon, I'll submit a more generic function to semTools that will accept any number of fitted lavaan objects, sort them according to the number of degrees of freedom, make the necessary tests, and return a logical matrix indicating the nesting/equivalence relationships. > I'm not even sure that it is sensible to want to constrain the total variance of endogenous latent variables to be 1, so I'd be interested to hear opinions on that.

Ultimately, the choice of metric for our latent variables is arbitrary because we haven't observed them, so we don't know what their metric really is.  We just want to choose something either meaningful (using marker indicators, which I think is dubious) or interpretable (using standard normal latent variables).  You can fix the latent residual variance to whatever you like just to fit the model, and then you can interpret the residual variance in the standardized solution, which is it's R-squared minus 1 (i.e., a standardized MS-error).  If you want the raw estimate to be standardized as well (for significance testing, I suppose?), then you can label the residual variance and use a model constraint statement to make the total variance 1 (although if you have a small residual variance, sampling error might yield negative residual variances on occasion, and that would cause problems here):

syntax <- "

F1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3

F2 =~ x4 + x5 + x6

F2 ~ Beta*F1
F1 ~~ 1*F1
F2 ~~ ResVar*F2

## MODEL CONSTRAINTS:
ResVar == 1 - Beta^2
"

Terry
